site.statement: Not your generic acads drive. You know that stuff already. This is everything else.
site.intro: Interviews, roles, internships, higher studies, the playlists worth your time, the tools to learn and the projects that actually teach you something. Sorted by the three directions an electronics career usually takes.

tracks.name: Analog
tracks.blurb: Circuits, RF, power and analog IC design. The continuous world, and the careers built on it.

primer.lead: Analog is the art of working with a continuous, imperfect world. Signals are voltages and currents that can take any value, every component is non-ideal, and every design is a negotiation between competing goals.
philosophy: In analog design nothing comes for free. Gain, bandwidth, noise, linearity, power, supply voltage and area all pull against each other, and improving one almost always costs another. The job is to find the best compromise for one specific application.

Good analog engineers think in approximations first. They size a circuit with hand calculations and intuition, know roughly what answer to expect, and only then use simulation to confirm it. A simulator tells you what happens; understanding tells you why.
Analog is where electronics meets the physical world. Every sensor, radio, power supply and audio path starts or ends in analog, so even the most digital system depends on someone who understands it.

work.title: Specify
work.text: Turn a system need into numbers: gain, bandwidth, noise, power, supply range, temperature range.

work.title: Choose and size
work.text: Pick a circuit topology and size transistors and passives with hand analysis.

work.title: Simulate
work.text: Check it in SPICE across DC, AC, transient and noise, then across process corners, temperature and mismatch.

work.title: Lay it out
work.text: Draw the physical layout with matching, symmetry and parasitics in mind, then re-simulate with extracted parasitics.

work.title: Verify and tape out
work.text: Pass design-rule and layout-versus-schematic checks and sign off before fabrication.

work.title: Bring up the silicon
work.text: Measure real chips or boards in the lab, compare against simulation and debug the gaps.

roles.name: Analog IC design engineer
roles.does: Designs amplifiers, voltage references, data converters, PLLs and other blocks at transistor level.

roles.name: Analog layout engineer
roles.does: Turns schematics into physical layout, handling matching, parasitics and design rules.

roles.name: RF and mixed-signal engineer
roles.does: Designs radio front ends (LNAs, mixers, oscillators) or ADCs and DACs that bridge analog and digital.

roles.name: Power electronics / power management engineer
roles.does: Designs DC-DC converters, regulators and battery chargers, on chips or on boards.

roles.name: Board-level hardware engineer
roles.does: Designs PCBs and signal chains: sensor front ends, filters, power rails.
roles.tools: KiCad or Altium, LTspice, lab instruments

roles.name: Characterization / validation engineer
roles.does: Tests silicon in the lab against its spec and automates measurements.

career.name: Core analog interviews
career.about: What core electronics companies ask in analog and circuit rounds, and how to prepare for them in four to six weeks.
career.why: Analog questions show up in nearly every core hardware interview, even for digital and embedded roles. Doing well here opens the most doors.

topics: CS / CG / CD gain by inspection

notes.title: Fundamentals of Microelectronics
notes.note: The best book for building the intuition interviewers test.

notes.title: Microelectronic Circuits
notes.note: Use it for depth on any topic you get stuck on.

notes.title: The Art of Electronics
notes.note: Practical, real-world circuits. Great for 'how would you build this' questions.

playlists.title: Electronics 1 and 2 lectures
playlists.note: Watch the amplifier and frequency-response lectures first.

playlists.title: Analog circuits explained
playlists.note: Quick refreshers on individual circuits the night before.

tips.text: Say your reasoning out loud. They care more about how you approach a circuit than the final number.
Practise finding gain by inspection until it's instant. It comes up in almost every round.
Have one project you can explain down to the component values. They will dig into it.

tracks.name: Digital
tracks.blurb: RTL, verification, physical design and processors. Ones and zeros, all the way down to silicon.

primer.lead: Digital design is about building enormous systems out of simple, reliable pieces. You describe behaviour at a high level, tools turn it into billions of transistors, and the hard part is making sure it is correct, fast enough and efficient.
philosophy: Abstraction is everything. Engineers describe hardware in RTL (Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL), and synthesis and place-and-route tools turn that into gates and wires. Each layer hides the one below so that very large designs stay manageable.
Correctness comes first. A bug in silicon can cost months and millions to fix, so verification often takes more engineering effort than the design itself.

Every design balances power, performance and area (PPA), all governed by the clock. Meeting timing, so every signal arrives before the next clock edge, is a constant theme from architecture to sign-off.

work.title: Architecture
work.text: Define what the chip or block does, its interfaces and its performance targets.

work.title: RTL design
work.text: Write synthesizable hardware descriptions of the micro-architecture.

work.title: Verification
work.text: Build testbenches, often in SystemVerilog and UVM, and drive coverage until you trust the design.

work.title: Synthesis and timing
work.text: Map RTL to a standard-cell library and check timing with static timing analysis.

work.title: Physical design
work.text: Floorplan, place, build the clock tree and route, then close timing and power.

work.title: Sign-off and silicon
work.text: Pass physical and electrical checks, tape out, and validate the returned silicon.

roles.name: RTL / design engineer
roles.does: Writes and owns the RTL for blocks such as interfaces, pipelines and controllers.

roles.name: Design verification (DV) engineer
roles.does: Builds testbenches and coverage models and finds bugs before tape-out. One of the largest hiring areas.

roles.name: Physical design engineer
roles.does: Takes the netlist to a routed layout that meets timing, power and area.

roles.name: DFT engineer
roles.does: Adds test structures (scan chains, BIST) so manufactured chips can be tested.

roles.name: FPGA engineer
roles.does: Implements designs on FPGAs for prototyping, defence, telecom and finance.

roles.name: Post-silicon validation engineer
roles.does: Tests real chips in the lab and debugs what simulation missed.

tracks.name: Embedded
tracks.blurb: Firmware, microcontrollers and real-time systems. Where hardware meets code and ships in products.

primer.lead: Embedded engineering is writing software for hardware that has a job to do: a car's brake controller, a pacemaker, a drone, a smartwatch. It lives close to the metal, with limited memory, power and time.
philosophy: Constraints define the work. You may have kilobytes of RAM, a battery that has to last a year, or a deadline measured in microseconds. Efficiency and predictability matter more than features.
Reliability beats cleverness. Embedded devices often can't be easily updated and failures can be dangerous, so simple, testable, well-understood code wins.
You work across the hardware-software line. You read datasheets and schematics as often as code, and debugging can mean a debugger, a logic analyser and an oscilloscope on the same problem.

work.title: Pick the hardware
work.text: Choose a microcontroller or processor, peripherals and power budget for the product.

work.title: Bring up the board
work.text: Get clocks, power and a debug connection (JTAG or SWD) working, then the first blinking LED.

work.title: Write drivers
work.text: Talk to peripherals: GPIO, timers, UART, SPI, I2C, ADC, DMA and interrupts.

work.title: Build the application
work.text: Structure the firmware, often on an RTOS such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr, with tasks and deadlines.

work.title: Test
work.text: Unit tests, hardware-in-the-loop tests and long soak tests on real devices.

work.title: Ship and maintain
work.text: Optimise power, add bootloaders and over-the-air updates, and meet safety or certification standards.

roles.name: Firmware engineer
roles.does: Writes low-level C/C++ for microcontrollers: drivers, peripherals, power management.
roles.tools: C, Keil or GCC, JTAG debuggers

roles.name: Embedded software engineer
roles.does: Builds the application layer on top of an RTOS: scheduling, communication, state machines.

roles.name: Embedded Linux / BSP engineer
roles.does: Brings up Linux on custom boards: bootloaders, device trees, kernel drivers.

roles.name: Automotive embedded engineer
roles.does: Develops ECU software under automotive standards and safety rules.

roles.name: IoT engineer
roles.does: Connects devices: BLE, Wi-Fi, cellular, cloud protocols, low-power design.

roles.name: Embedded test / validation engineer
roles.does: Builds test rigs and automated hardware-in-the-loop tests.
